teile.einleitung: The Four Sights are a well-known story from the life of Prince Siddhartha Gautama, who later became the Buddha. On four trips out of the palace he met the suffering of people. These encounters changed his life.
wichtigste: Siddhartha grew up as a prince, sheltered in a palace.
On the first trip he saw an old man.
On the second he saw a sick person.
On the third he saw a dead person.
On the fourth he saw a calm monk.
At about 29 he secretly left the palace at night.

abschnitte.text: According to tradition, **Siddhartha Gautama** was the son of a king. His father wanted him never to see anything sad. That is why Siddhartha lived in a magnificent **palace** with everything he wished for. Nobody who was old, sick or sad was supposed to meet him. But one day he wanted to get to know the world outside.

On the **first trip** Siddhartha saw a very old man. In this way he learned that all people grow **old**. On the **second** he met a sick person and understood that anyone can fall **ill**. On the **third** he saw a dead person. Then he recognised that every life one day **ends**.

On the **fourth trip** Siddhartha saw a calm, peaceful **monk**. He owned almost nothing and yet seemed content. The monk showed him that there might be a **way** of dealing with suffering. Siddhartha decided to seek this way himself.

At about **29**, Siddhartha secretly left the palace **at night**. He rode away on his white horse **Kanthaka**, accompanied by his servant **Channa**. Afterwards he cut off his long **hair**. This showed that he no longer wanted to be a prince. He now lived as a wandering seeker and years later found enlightenment.

gewusst: Buddhists call the departure from the palace “the great renunciation”.
The Four Sights are shown in pictures and reliefs in many temples in Asia.

teile.einleitung: Yoga is an ancient teaching from India. It combines body postures, conscious breathing and calm. Today people all over the world practise yoga, including in many Swiss schools and gyms.
wichtigste: Yoga comes from India and is over 2,000 years old.
The body postures are called asanas.
In yoga you pay special attention to the breath.
The sun salutation is a well-known sequence of postures.
In the tree pose you stand on one leg.
International Yoga Day is on 21 June.
People usually practise on a mat.

abschnitte.text: Yoga arose in **India** and has been practised there for well over **2,000 years**. Ancient texts describe it, such as the **Yoga Sutras** of Patanjali. Originally yoga was a path to inner calm and insight. It plays a role in **Hinduism** and also in other Indian religions. The word yoga comes from Sanskrit and means roughly “to join”.

The body postures in yoga are called **asanas**. You hold them quietly for a while. While doing so you breathe **calmly** and **consciously**, because breath and movement belong together. The breathing exercises are called **pranayama**. Many people do yoga to become more flexible, stronger and more relaxed.

The **sun salutation** is a series of postures one after another. Many do it in the morning. In the **tree** you stand on one leg, with the other foot resting against the leg and the arms going up. In the **cobra** you lie on your stomach and lift your upper body like a snake. Many postures are named after animals or plants, for example downward-facing dog.

Today yoga is practised **all over the world**. It is usually done on a thin **mat** so that you do not slip. The **United Nations** declared **21 June** International Yoga Day. It has been celebrated since **2015**. In Switzerland too there are many yoga classes, for children as well as for adults.

gewusst: 21 June was chosen for Yoga Day because in the Northern Hemisphere it is the longest day of the year.
Since 2016 yoga has been part of UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage.

teile.einleitung: Voltaire was a French writer and philosopher of the Enlightenment. He lived from 1694 to 1778 and fought with a sharp pen for tolerance and against religious fanaticism. For many years he lived very close to Geneva.
wichtigste: Voltaire was really called François-Marie Arouet.
He is among the best-known thinkers of the Enlightenment.
His battle cry was “Écrasez l’infâme!”.
Because of the Calas affair, he wrote the “Traité sur la tolérance” in 1763.
In “Candide” he mocked the teaching of the best of all possible worlds.
From about 1760 he lived for around 18 years in Ferney near Geneva.
He rejected the Church but, as a deist, believed in a creator god.

abschnitte.text: Voltaire’s name by birth was **François-Marie Arouet**. From 1718 he called himself Voltaire. He wrote plays, poems, novels and countless letters. He belonged to the **Enlightenment**, a movement that relied on **reason** instead of blind obedience. His texts were often witty and mocking.

Voltaire fought against **superstition** and the intolerance of the Church of his time. His battle cry was **“Écrasez l’infâme!”**, that is, “Crush the infamous thing”. The **Calas affair** became well known: the Protestant Jean Calas was wrongly condemned and executed in Toulouse in 1762. Voltaire campaigned for his name to be cleared. In 1763 he wrote the **“Traité sur la tolérance”** about it, a work on tolerance.

In **1755** a huge **earthquake** destroyed the city of **Lisbon**, and tens of thousands died. Voltaire asked himself how a kind God could allow such a thing. He wrote a poem about the catastrophe. In 1759 his novel **“Candide”** appeared. In it the teacher Pangloss claims, despite all misfortunes, that this is the **best of all possible worlds**. In this way Voltaire mocked the optimism of the philosopher **Leibniz**.

Voltaire first lived in the house **“Les Délices”** in **Geneva**. Around 1760 he moved to his château in **Ferney**, just across the border in France. He lived there for about 18 years. The nearness of the border was practical: if there was trouble, he could quickly move out of reach. In his honour the place is now called **Ferney-Voltaire**.

Voltaire was a sharp **critic of the Church**, but not an atheist. He was a **deist**: he believed in a creator god but rejected miracles and church teachings. Famous is his sentence **“If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.”** He held belief in God to be reasonable and useful for morality.

gewusst: In Geneva, Voltaire’s former house “Les Délices” is now a museum.
Many thousands of Voltaire’s letters survive; among others he corresponded with the Prussian king Frederick the Great.

teile.einleitung: Thailand is a country in South-East Asia in which most people are Buddhists. Religion shapes many customs in everyday life there. Anyone visiting Thailand should know a few rules of respect.
wichtigste: The great majority of people in Thailand are Buddhists.
Theravada Buddhism predominates.
The head is regarded as the most valuable part of the body; you do not touch it on others.
The feet are regarded as the lowest part; you do not point them at people or Buddha figures.
To greet someone you put your palms together, which is called the wai.

abschnitte.text: In Thailand the great majority of people are **Buddhist**. **Theravada Buddhism**, the “teaching of the elders”, predominates. All over the country there are numerous temples, called **wat** in Thai. In the morning monks in orange robes walk through the streets, and people give them food. Many young men live for a time as monks in a monastery. Muslims, Christians and members of other religions also live in Thailand.

In Thailand the **head** is regarded as the most valuable and highest part of the body. That is why you do not touch another person’s head, not even a child’s. The **feet**, by contrast, are regarded as the lowest part. You do not point your feet at people or **Buddha figures** and you do not put them on the table. Before entering a temple or a home you take your shoes off.

To greet someone in Thailand you put your palms together in front of your chest and bow your head slightly. This gesture is called the **wai**. The higher you hold your hands, the more respect you show. In front of monks and older people the wai is especially deep. Raising your voice or showing anger in front of others is regarded as impolite.

gewusst: In front of many houses in Thailand there is a small spirit house on a post, in which flowers and food are placed for the protective spirits.

teile.einleitung: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods. He ruled over gods and humans from Mount Olympus. When he was angry, he hurled lightning bolts down to earth.
wichtigste: Zeus was the most powerful god of the ancient Greeks.
He was the god of the sky and the weather.
His sign is the lightning bolt, his sacred animal the eagle.
His wife was Hera, the goddess of marriage.
His father was the Titan Cronus, his mother Rhea.
The ancient Olympic Games took place in his honour.
The statue of Zeus at Olympia was one of the seven wonders of the world.

abschnitte.text: **Zeus** was the god of the **sky** and the **weather**. He ruled over all gods and humans. According to belief, the gods lived on **Mount Olympus**, the highest mountain in Greece. When Zeus was angry, he threw **lightning bolts** down to earth. The lightning bolt was therefore his most important sign.

Zeus was the son of the Titan **Cronus** and of **Rhea**. According to the legend, Cronus feared that one of his children would overthrow him. Rhea therefore hid the little Zeus on the island of **Crete**. When Zeus was grown up, he defeated his father and the Titans. Afterwards he became **king of the gods**.

The wife of Zeus was **Hera**. She was the queen of the gods and the goddess of **marriage**. The **eagle**, his sacred animal, belonged to Zeus. As king of the birds, it suited the king of the gods well. To the Romans, Zeus was **Jupiter**.

In **Olympia** stood a great sanctuary of Zeus. There, in his honour, the ancient **Olympic Games** took place, the first recorded one in 776 BC. In the temple stood a huge **statue** of Zeus made of **gold** and **ivory**. It was the work of the sculptor **Phidias**. It was counted among the **seven wonders** of the ancient world but has not survived.

gewusst: The statue of Zeus at Olympia was about 12 metres high.
The planet Jupiter bears the Roman name of Zeus.

teile.einleitung: The Vestal Virgins were priestesses in ancient Rome. They served the goddess Vesta and guarded the sacred fire of the city. They enjoyed great respect.
wichtigste: Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth fire.
The Vestal Virgins guarded the sacred fire in the Temple of Vesta.
Usually six Vestals served at the same time.
Their service lasted 30 years.
They were chosen as girls aged 6 to 10.
The head was called the Virgo Vestalis Maxima.
They lived in the Atrium Vestae next to the round Temple of Vesta.

abschnitte.text: **Vesta** was the goddess of the **hearth fire**. In ancient Rome the hearth was the centre of every house. In the Temple of Vesta a **sacred fire** burned for the whole city. It was never allowed to go out. Otherwise the Romans feared great misfortune for Rome.

The Vestal Virgins were chosen already as girls, aged **6 to 10**. They came from respected families. The chief priest, the **Pontifex Maximus**, made the choice. The service lasted **30 years**: ten years of learning, ten years of serving, ten years of teaching the younger ones. After that they were allowed to leave the temple.

Usually there were **six** Vestal Virgins at the same time. The oldest and most experienced led the group. She was called the **Virgo Vestalis Maxima**. The Vestals had rights that other women in Rome did not have. They were allowed, for example, to control their own property and had seats of honour at the games.

The **Temple of Vesta** in the **Roman Forum** was **round**. The round shape was meant to recall old round huts. In its middle burned the fire. Right next to it lay the priestesses’ residence, the **Atrium Vestae**. Its remains and statues can still be visited in Rome today.

gewusst: In the temple the Vestals also guarded secret sacred objects that only they were allowed to see.
The cult of Vesta lasted over a thousand years, until it was banned at the end of the 4th century AD.

teile.einleitung: Theodor Herzl was a journalist and writer from Vienna. He is regarded as the founder of political Zionism, that is, the movement for a Jewish state of its own. He held the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897.
wichtigste: Theodor Herzl was born in 1860 in Pest, which today belongs to Budapest.
As a correspondent of the Viennese “Neue Freie Presse” he experienced the Dreyfus Affair in Paris.
His book “The Jewish State” appeared in 1896.
In 1897 the First Zionist Congress took place in Basel.
His novel “Altneuland” of 1902 carries the motto “If you will it, it is no fairy tale”.
Herzl died in 1904, and the State of Israel was founded in 1948.

abschnitte.text: Theodor Herzl was born in **1860** in **Pest**, which today belongs to **Budapest** in Hungary. As a teenager he moved with his family to **Vienna**. There he studied law and began to write. He wrote plays and newspaper articles and became a well-known journalist.

From 1891 Herzl reported from **Paris** for the Viennese newspaper **“Neue Freie Presse”**. There he witnessed the trial of the Jewish officer **Alfred Dreyfus**, who was wrongly accused of treason. Herzl saw how strong **antisemitism**, that is, hatred of Jews, was even in France. This strengthened him in the idea that the Jews needed a state of their own.

In **1896** Herzl published the book **“The Jewish State”**. In it he described how a state of their own for Jews could come about. This movement is called **Zionism**, after Zion, another name for Jerusalem. Herzl travelled to rulers and politicians to win support. Many laughed at him, others were enthusiastic.

From 29 to 31 August **1897** the **First Zionist Congress** took place in **Basel**, in the Stadtcasino. Around 200 participants from many countries came together. Afterwards Herzl wrote in his diary: “At Basel I founded the Jewish State.” He added that everyone would laugh at this, but that in 50 years it would be seen. A good 50 years later, in **1948**, **Israel** was founded.

In 1902 Herzl’s novel **“Altneuland”** appeared. In it he describes a modern Jewish society in **Palestine**. The motto is: “If you will it, it is no fairy tale.” The Hebrew title of the book is **Tel Aviv**, and a city was later given that name. Herzl died already in **1904** in Austria, at only 44 years old.

gewusst: The Zionist Congress later took place in Basel several more times, more often than in any other city.
Herzl’s remains were transferred to Jerusalem in 1949; the site of his grave is now called Mount Herzl.

teile.einleitung: The Vedas are the oldest holy scriptures of Hinduism. They consist of hymns, prayers and instructions for sacrificial ceremonies. For many centuries they were passed on only orally.
wichtigste: The word “Veda” comes from Sanskrit and means “knowledge”.
There are four Vedas: Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda.
The Rigveda is the oldest and probably arose from about 1500 to 1200 BC.
The Rigveda contains over a thousand hymns to gods.
Agni, the god of fire, is invoked very often.
Indra is sung about in most of the hymns of the Rigveda.
Priests learned the verses by heart and passed them on orally.

abschnitte.text: “Veda” means “knowledge” in **Sanskrit**. What is meant is a holy knowledge that, according to Hindu belief, was not invented by humans. Wise seers are said to have “heard” it. That is why the Vedas are also called **shruti**, what is heard. They form the basis of many later Hindu teachings.

The **Rigveda** is a collection of hymns. The **Samaveda** contains melodies with which the verses were sung. The **Yajurveda** describes formulas and actions for sacrificial ceremonies. The **Atharvaveda** contains, among other things, blessings for everyday life. Together they form the four Vedas.

The Rigveda consists of over a thousand **hymns** that praise gods. Most often sung about is **Indra**, the god of storms and war, in about a quarter of all hymns. Very often invoked too is **Agni**, the god of fire. According to the Vedic idea, Agni carries the offerings to the gods. **Varuna** is also one of the important gods.

Long before the Vedas were written down, they were passed on **orally**. Priests learned the verses syllable by syllable **by heart**. With special methods of learning they made sure that no word was changed. In this way the texts remained astonishingly exact for many centuries. To this day priests recite the verses at ceremonies.

gewusst: The oral tradition of the Vedas is part of UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage.
The Rigveda is regarded as one of the oldest religious texts in the world that is still used today.

teile.einleitung: Totemism is the name for the belief that a group of people is especially connected with an animal, a plant or another being. This being is called a totem. Researchers such as Émile Durkheim and Claude Lévi-Strauss dealt intensively with totemism.
wichtigste: The word “totem” comes from the language of the Ojibwe in North America.
A totem is an animal, a plant or a being that stands for a group.
In 1912, in “The Elementary Forms of Religious Life”, Émile Durkheim developed a theory about it.
For Durkheim, the distinction between sacred and profane is the core of every religion.
According to Durkheim, the totem ultimately symbolises the clan, that is, society.
In 1962 Claude Lévi-Strauss criticised totemism as an artificial category of research.

abschnitte.text: The word **“totem”** goes back to an expression of the **Ojibwe**, also called Anishinaabe, in **North America**. It means roughly “his relative”. In the 18th century the word came to Europe through traders’ reports. A totem is an animal, a plant or another being with which a group, a **clan**, feels especially connected. Often there are rules, for example that you may not hunt the totem animal.

The French sociologist **Émile Durkheim** published the work **“The Elementary Forms of Religious Life”** in **1912**. In it he studied religion on the basis of reports about **Australian clans**. At the centre is the distinction between **sacred** and **profane**: all religions divide the world into a sacred and an everyday sphere. Sacred things are set apart and protected by prohibitions.

abschnitte.titel: The totem as an image of the group
abschnitte.text: Durkheim interpreted the totem as an **emblem**, that is, a sign of the group. Anyone who reveres the totem is, according to Durkheim, basically revering their **own community**. In this way religion strengthens **social cohesion**. At great ritual festivals a stirring shared excitement arises. Durkheim called it **collective effervescence**, and saw in it the origin of the experience of the sacred.

Durkheim defined religion as a system of **beliefs** and **practices** that unites all its followers in one moral community. He called this community a **church**, even though it need have nothing to do with a Christian church. In this way he set religion apart from private **magic**, which individuals practise for themselves.

In **1962**, in his book “Totemism”, the ethnologist **Claude Lévi-Strauss** criticised the whole idea. He thought that totemism was an **artificial category** of research that throws very different things together. Animals served not primarily as revered beings but as **tools for thinking**, for distinguishing social groups from one another. Animals, he said, are “good to think with”.

gewusst: Many sports clubs and scout groups carry an animal as an emblem, which some researchers compare with totems.
Durkheim relied above all on reports about the Arrernte in central Australia.

teile.einleitung: The Temple in Jerusalem was the central sanctuary of ancient Israel. There were two temples one after the other, and both were destroyed. In Judaism they are remembered to this day.
wichtigste: According to the Bible, King Solomon, the son of David, had the first temple built.
The Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed it in 586 BC.
After the return from Babylon, a second temple was built.
The Romans under Titus destroyed the second temple in AD 70.
On the fast day of Tisha B’Av, Jews remember the destruction of both temples.
The Western Wall is a remnant of the wall around the Temple Mount.

abschnitte.text: According to the Bible, King **Solomon**, the son of King **David**, had a magnificent temple built on a hill in Jerusalem. That is why it is also called **Solomon’s Temple**. In the innermost room, the **Holy of Holies**, stood, according to the Bible, the **Ark of the Covenant** with the tablets of the law. Only the high priest was allowed in there, once a year. In the Temple priests offered sacrifices and prayers were said.

In **586 BC** the army of the Babylonian king **Nebuchadnezzar II** conquered Jerusalem. The **Babylonians** destroyed the city and the Temple. Many people were carried off to **Babylon**. This time is called the **Babylonian Exile**. When the Persians conquered Babylon, the exiles were allowed to return.

After the return, the Jews built a new temple, at first a modest one. It was consecrated around **515 BC**. Much later King **Herod** had it magnificently extended and the Temple Mount enlarged with enormous walls. In the **Jewish War** against Rome, the Romans under **Titus** conquered Jerusalem in **AD 70** and destroyed the Temple. It was never rebuilt.

Part of the western retaining wall of the Temple Mount survived. It is called the **Western Wall** or **Wailing Wall** and is today the most important place of prayer for Jews. Many visitors push small notes with prayers into the cracks between the stones. On the Temple Mount itself stand today the **Dome of the Rock** and the **Al-Aqsa Mosque**, which are holy to Muslims.

On **Tisha B’Av**, the ninth day of the Jewish month of Av, Jews remember the destruction of both temples. It is a **fast day** on which people eat and drink nothing. In the synagogue the **Book of Lamentations** from the Bible is read. The day usually falls in July or August.

gewusst: In Rome the Arch of Titus still stands today, on which soldiers carry off the seven-armed candelabrum from the Temple.
Some stones of the Western Wall weigh many tonnes and date from the time of Herod.

teile.einleitung: The baptismal candle is a special candle that a child receives at a Christian baptism. It recalls the light that, according to Christian belief, comes from Jesus Christ. Many families keep it for a lifetime.
wichtigste: At a Christian baptism the child receives a baptismal candle of its own.
The baptismal candle is usually lit from the church’s great Easter candle.
The light stands for Jesus Christ, who is called the “light of the world” in the Bible.
Often the name and the date of baptism are on the candle.
Many light the candle again on every baptism anniversary.

abschnitte.text: During the **baptism** the child receives a candle of its own. Usually the godmother or godfather, that is, the baptismal sponsors, or a parent lights it from the church’s great **Easter candle**. The light is a sign of **Jesus Christ**. In the Bible Jesus says: “I am the light of the world.” The candle is meant to show that this light now accompanies the child’s life too.

abschnitte.titel: What a baptismal candle looks like
abschnitte.text: Baptismal candles are often white and decorated with wax. Many bear the child’s **name** and the **date of the baptism**. Popular are Christian signs such as the **cross**, the **fish**, a **dove**, water waves or a rainbow. Some families design the candle themselves, others buy it ready decorated. In Switzerland baptismal candles are found in Catholic and in many Reformed parishes.

After the baptism the family takes the candle home. Many light it again on every **baptism anniversary**, that is, on the anniversary of the baptism. Sometimes it is also lit on other big days, for example at **first communion** or **confirmation**. In this way the candle recalls that the child belongs to the Christian community.

gewusst: The Easter candle from which baptismal candles are lit often bears the Greek letters alpha and omega, the first and the last letters of the alphabet.

teile.einleitung: Tenrikyo is a religion from Japan that arose in the 19th century. It goes back to a farmer’s wife named Nakayama Miki. At its centre is the idea that all people should lead a joyful life.
wichtigste: Tenrikyo was founded by Nakayama Miki, whom her followers call Oyasama.
The founding day is regarded as 26 October 1838.
The centre is the Jiba in the city of Tenri, where humans are said to have been created.
The goal is the “joyful life” of all people.
The body is regarded as lent by God.
According to the teaching, eight kinds of “dust” cloud the mind.
The most important scripture is the Ofudesaki.

abschnitte.text: **Nakayama Miki** was a farmer’s wife from the area of **Nara** in Japan. According to tradition, on **26 October 1838** God spoke through her, and she began to teach. This date is regarded as the founding day of Tenrikyo. Her followers lovingly call her **Oyasama**. She helped many people and shared her possessions with the poor.

The most important place of Tenrikyo is the **Jiba**. There God is said to have created humans. It lies in the headquarters of the religion in the city of **Tenri**, which is named after the religion. At the Jiba stands the pillar **Kanrodai**. Many followers travel there to “return home”, as they call it.

According to the teaching, God created humans in order to see their **joyful life** and to share their joy. To this end, people are to free their minds from **selfishness** and **greed**. The **body** is regarded as **“something lent”** by God; only the mind belongs to the person themselves. That is why you should use the body with gratitude and care.

Tenrikyo speaks of **eight kinds of dust** that cloud the mind. They include **miserliness**, **covetousness**, **hatred** and **arrogance**, among others. Like dust in the house, they are to be swept away regularly. This is done by reflecting on your own behaviour and by helping others.

The most important scripture is the **Ofudesaki**, which means “tip of the brush”. The founder wrote it herself, and it comprises around 1,700 verses in poetic form. Besides it there is the **Mikagura-uta**, a collection of songs for services with dance, and the **Osashizu** with further instructions.

gewusst: The city of Tenri is one of the few cities in Japan that are named after a religion.

teile.einleitung: Vajrayana is a form of Buddhism that is widespread especially in Tibet, in the Himalayas and in Mongolia. The name means “diamond vehicle”. In Japan too there is a form of it, the Shingon school.
wichtigste: Vajrayana means “diamond vehicle”: vajra means thunderbolt or diamond, yana means vehicle.
In ritual, the vajra and the bell are used together.
Padmasambhava is revered as “Guru Rinpoche”.
Nyingma is regarded as the oldest of the four great Tibetan schools.
Milarepa was a pupil of the translator Marpa.
Atisha came to Tibet in 1042.
In Japan, Kukai founded the Shingon school in the 9th century.

abschnitte.text: **Vajra** means **thunderbolt** or **diamond** and stands for indestructibility. **Yana** means **vehicle**, that is, a path to liberation. Vajrayana uses special methods such as **mantras**, rituals, meditation with inner images and **mandalas**. In ritual, monks usually hold the **vajra** in the right hand and the **bell**, called a **ghanta**, in the left. The vajra stands for method and compassion, the bell for **wisdom**.

**Padmasambhava** is revered as **“Guru Rinpoche”**. He is said to have come to Tibet in the 8th century and to have helped in building the monastery of **Samye**. The **Nyingma** school traces itself back to this first spread; its name means “the ancient ones”. It is regarded as the oldest of the four great schools. In **1042** the Bengali scholar **Atisha** came to Tibet and shaped the second spread. The **Kadampa** school goes back to his pupils.

**Milarepa** lived in the 11th and 12th centuries and was a pupil of the translator **Marpa**. Marpa put him through hard tests before he taught him. Afterwards Milarepa meditated for many years in caves in the mountains. He became one of the great masters of the **Kagyu** tradition. His songs, the **“Hundred Thousand Songs”**, are very well known in Tibet.

A **mandala** is an artful, round picture that represents an ordered world. For a **sand mandala**, monks scatter fine coloured sand into a pattern, often over days. When it is finished it is **destroyed** and the sand swept together. Often the sand is then put into a body of water. This shows **impermanence**: nothing in the world lasts for ever.

In Japan too there is a form of Vajrayana. The monk **Kukai**, also called **Kobo Daishi**, learned esoteric teachings in **China**, that is, teachings passed on only to the initiated. In the **9th century** he then founded the **Shingon** school. Its centre is **Mount Koya**, south of Osaka, where many temples still stand.

gewusst: On Mount Koya, visitors can spend the night in temples and take part in the monks’ morning prayer.
Shingon means “true word” and is the Japanese translation for mantra.

teile.einleitung: Zhuangzi was a Daoist thinker in ancient China who lived from about 365 to 290 BC. A famous book full of parables and stories is also named after him. It asks with humour about freedom, knowledge and the natural course of things.
wichtigste: Zhuangzi lived in the 4th century BC in the Warring States period.
In its surviving version the book Zhuangzi has 33 chapters.
Famous is the parable of the butterfly dream.
The cook Ding carves up an ox so skilfully that his knife never goes blunt.
With his friend Huizi, Zhuangzi argued about the joy of the fish.
The giant fish Kun and the giant bird Peng stand for boundless freedom.
Zhuangzi preferred a free life to a ministerial post.

abschnitte.text: **Zhuangzi** lived from about **365 to 290 BC**, in the time of the **Warring States**. He was a contemporary of the Confucian **Mencius**. Alongside Laozi, he is regarded as the most important thinker of **Daoism**. In the version by Guo Xiang, the book **Zhuangzi** has **33 chapters**. The seven **inner chapters** are regarded as the oldest part.

The best-known parable is the **butterfly dream**. Zhuangzi dreamt that he was a **butterfly** fluttering about happily. When he woke, he asked himself: am I Zhuangzi, who dreamt he was a butterfly? Or am I a butterfly dreaming that I am Zhuangzi? The parable questions the fixed boundary between self and world.

The **cook Ding** carves up an ox so skilfully that his knife never goes blunt. He does not cut against bones but follows the natural **gaps**. The image shows effortless mastery in harmony with the **Dao**. In another story, Zhuangzi and his friend **Huizi** stand on a bridge. Huizi asks how Zhuangzi knows that the **fish** are happy, and so a famous conversation arises about the limits of knowledge.

The first chapter is called **“Free and Easy Wandering”**. In it the giant fish **Kun** changes into the enormous bird **Peng**. It flies thousands of miles. Small creatures laugh at it because they cannot imagine such a flight. Kun and Peng stand for **boundless freedom** and a wide view.

According to legend, Zhuangzi was offered a **ministerial post**. He answered with an image: a dead sacred **tortoise** is revered in the temple. A living one, however, would rather drag its tail through the **mud**. In this way he preferred **freedom** to fame. He also saw **death** calmly: when his wife died, he drummed on a bowl and sang, for death was only a **transformation** like the change of the seasons.

gewusst: The butterfly dream is among the best-known stories in Chinese literature.
In the 8th century the book Zhuangzi was given the honorific title “True Scripture of Southern Florescence” in China.

teile.einleitung: Vaisakhi is a spring festival from the Punjab, a region in the north of India and Pakistan. Originally it is a harvest festival. For the Sikhs it is also one of the most important holidays, because on this day in 1699 the Khalsa was founded.
wichtigste: In the Punjab, Vaisakhi is originally a harvest festival and at the same time a New Year festival.
It usually falls on 13 or 14 April.
At this time the wheat is harvested in the Punjab.
On Vaisakhi in 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa.
In the Nagar Kirtan the congregation walks singing through the streets.
In front of the gurdwara the flag and its cloth on the pole are renewed.
The folk dance bhangra is often part of the festival.

abschnitte.text: In the **Punjab**, **Vaisakhi** is an old **harvest festival**. In April the **winter wheat** is ripe there, and the farmers celebrate the end of the harvest. Vaisakhi is at the same time a **New Year festival** according to the solar calendar. That is why it falls almost always on **13 or 14 April**. It is celebrated with markets, music and good food.

For the **Sikhs**, Vaisakhi has a special meaning. On Vaisakhi in **1699**, **Guru Gobind Singh**, the tenth guru of the Sikhs, founded the **Khalsa**. This is the community of initiated Sikhs who commit themselves to certain rules. The first five men who declared themselves ready for this are called the **Panj Pyare**, the “five beloved ones”. That is why Vaisakhi is still one of the most important holidays for Sikhs today.

The house of worship of the Sikhs is called a **gurdwara**. In front of it stands a tall pole with a flag. On Vaisakhi the flag is taken down, the **pole is washed** and wrapped anew with cloth. Then a **new flag** is raised. In the gurdwara there are prayers, hymns and a shared meal that is open to all guests, whatever their religion.

In the **Nagar Kirtan** the congregation walks singing through the streets. Often five men in **orange** with swords lead the way, recalling the Panj Pyare. The cheerful folk dance **bhangra** is also part of the festival. It is a vigorous dance of the farmers of the Punjab and is danced at the harvest festival with large **drums**. In Switzerland too, Sikh communities celebrate Vaisakhi, for example at the gurdwara in Langenthal.

gewusst: The flag in front of a gurdwara is called the Nishan Sahib.
In cities such as London or Toronto, tens of thousands of people walk through the streets on Vaisakhi.

teile.einleitung: Zarathustra was a prophet in ancient Iran. He is regarded as the founder of Zoroastrianism, one of the oldest religions in the world, which reveres only one supreme god. His teaching places the struggle between good and evil at the centre.
wichtigste: In Greek, Zarathustra is called Zoroaster, hence the name Zoroastrianism.
The supreme god is called Ahura Mazda, “wise lord”.
His opponent is Angra Mainyu, later called Ahriman.
The guiding principle is: good thoughts, good words, good deeds.
The holy scripture is called the Avesta, and the Gathas are regarded as songs of Zarathustra.
The winged symbol is called the Faravahar.
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote the book “Thus Spoke Zarathustra”.

abschnitte.text: **Zarathustra** lived in ancient **Iran**. When exactly is disputed among scholars. In Greek he is called **Zoroaster**, hence the name **Zoroastrianism**. He taught that there is one supreme, good god. In Zoroastrianism **fire** plays an important role as a sign of purity.

The supreme god is called **Ahura Mazda**, which means “wise lord”. He is the creator and goodness itself. His opponent is **Angra Mainyu**, later called **Ahriman**. He stands for evil and destruction. In this struggle every person is to choose the good **freely**.

The most important guiding principle is: **good thoughts, good words, good deeds**. In Avestan this is **Humata, Hukhta, Hvarshta**. It means that a good person does not only act rightly. They should also think well and speak well. In this way everyone helps good to win.

The holy collection of writings is called the **Avesta**. It is written in an ancient Iranian language and was passed down **orally** for a long time. The oldest part is the **Gathas**, 17 hymns in a very archaic language. They are regarded as the words of Zarathustra himself. Today Zoroastrians live mainly in Iran and in India, where they are called **Parsis**.

The symbol of Zoroastrianism is the **Faravahar**. It shows a man with large wings and is today also a sign of Iranian culture. Zarathustra also became known in Europe. The German philosopher **Friedrich Nietzsche** wrote the book **“Thus Spoke Zarathustra”** between 1883 and 1885. In it he used the figure for his own ideas, not for the ancient religion.

gewusst: Nietzsche had the idea for “Thus Spoke Zarathustra” in the Upper Engadine, near Sils Maria.
The Persian new year festival Nowruz has roots in Zoroastrian times.

teile.einleitung: Vodun is a religion from West Africa that is widespread above all in Benin and Togo. It reveres spirits and deities connected with nature and the ancestors. Via the Caribbean, Voodoo in Haiti also arose from it.
wichtigste: The word Vodun comes from the language of the Fon and means roughly spirit or deity.
Every year on 10 January, Benin celebrates a national Voodoo holiday.
The coastal city of Ouidah is regarded as the most important centre.
In a temple in Ouidah, pythons are revered as sacred.
Enslaved people brought the faith to the Caribbean.
In Haitian Voodoo the spirit beings are called loa.
Voodoo dolls with pins come above all from films and novels.

abschnitte.text: The word **Vodun** comes from the language of the **Fon**. It means roughly **spirit** or **deity**. The Fon live mainly in present-day **Benin**. There the kingdom of **Dahomey** once lay, which existed from the 17th to the 19th century. In this kingdom, Vodun played an important role.

In Benin many people practise Vodun, often alongside Christianity or Islam. Since the 1990s, **10 January** has been a national holiday there, the “Fête du Vodoun”. The biggest celebrations take place in the coastal city of **Ouidah**. Ouidah was once also an important port of the **slave trade**. Today a monument there recalls the people who were taken away.

In Vodun there are many spirit beings who mediate between people and a supreme god. An important deity is **Legba**. He is regarded as a guardian who opens the **gate** between humans and spirits. That is why he is invoked first at ceremonies. In Ouidah stands a **python temple** in which many royal pythons live. The snakes are regarded as sacred and may not be killed.

From the 16th century many people from West Africa were taken to the Caribbean as **enslaved people**. They brought their faith with them. In **Haiti** it combined with elements of **Catholic** belief. In this way Haitian **Voodoo** arose. Its spirit beings are called **loa** or lwa, and each loa has its own colours, songs and signs.

Many people think of **dolls with pins** or of sorcery when they hear Voodoo. This picture was spread above all by **horror films** and novels. In traditional West African Vodun such dolls play hardly any role. For believers it is about community, healing, ancestors and respect for nature.

gewusst: Benin is one of the few countries in the world in which Vodun is celebrated as an official holiday.
In Ouidah the “Route des Esclaves” leads from the town centre to the beach, to the monument “Gate of No Return”.

teile.einleitung: Zen is a branch of Buddhism that is especially well known in Japan. At its centre are seated meditation and one’s own experience. Zen has also strongly shaped gardens, art and everyday life in Japan.
wichtigste: Zen is the Japanese pronunciation of the Chinese word Chan.
The word goes back to the Sanskrit word dhyana and means meditation.
Seated meditation is called zazen.
A koan is a puzzling question meant to break through habitual thinking.
According to legend, Bodhidharma brought Chan to China.
The two great schools in Japan are Rinzai and Soto.
Enlightenment is called satori in Zen.

abschnitte.titel: From India via China to Japan
abschnitte.text: The word **Zen** goes back to the Sanskrit word **dhyana**, which means meditation or absorption. In China it became **Chan**, in Japan **Zen**. According to legend, the Indian monk **Bodhidharma** brought this teaching to China. He is said to have meditated facing a wall for nine years. In the **12th and 13th centuries** the school came from China to **Japan**.

The most important practice in Zen is **zazen**, seated meditation. You sit still and upright, usually on a round **cushion**. Attention rests on your posture and your **breath**. You let thoughts come and go without clinging to them. The aim is to be completely in the present moment.

A **koan** is a puzzling question or short story. A well-known example runs: “What is the sound of one hand clapping?” Ordinary thinking finds no answer. Koans are meant to break through **habitual thinking**. According to the teaching, a sudden insight can then arise, the **satori**.

In Japan there are two great Zen schools. The **Rinzai school** works strongly with **koans**. The **Soto school** stresses “just sitting”, that is, zazen without a particular goal. Both schools have many temples and monasteries. There monks live by strict rules and combine meditation with work.

Zen has strongly shaped Japanese culture. Well known are the **Zen gardens** of raked gravel and stones. In the rock garden of the **Ryoan-ji** temple in Kyoto, **15 stones** lie in white gravel. The **tea ceremony**, calligraphy and flower arranging are also influenced by Zen. All of them demand calm and full attention.

gewusst: In Japan Bodhidharma is revered as Daruma, and the round red Daruma dolls are named after him.
In Switzerland too there are Zen groups and meditation centres that practise zazen.

teile.einleitung: Thich Nhat Hanh was a Buddhist monk from Vietnam. All his life he campaigned for peace and made mindfulness known worldwide. For many years he lived in exile in France.
wichtigste: Thich Nhat Hanh became known as the founder of “engaged Buddhism”.
In the mid-1960s he founded the School of Youth for Social Service.
In 1966 he founded the Order of Interbeing and went abroad.
In 1967 Martin Luther King nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 1982 he founded the monastery of Plum Village in south-western France.
Only in 2005 was he allowed to travel to Vietnam again.
He died in 2022 at the age of 95 in Hue.

abschnitte.text: Thich Nhat Hanh was born in Vietnam in 1926 and became a monk while still a teenager. During the **Vietnam War** he demanded that **meditation** be combined with work for **peace** and **social justice**. For this he coined the term **engaged Buddhism**. It grew into a worldwide movement. In the mid-1960s he founded the **School of Youth for Social Service**: young volunteers rebuilt schools and clinics in war-torn villages and helped refugees.

In **1966** he founded the **Order of Interbeing**, in Vietnamese **Tiep Hien**. It unites monks, nuns and lay people and is based on fourteen **mindfulness trainings**. In the same year he travelled abroad to campaign for peace. After that he was for a long time not allowed to return to his homeland. He lived almost 40 years in **exile**.

In the USA he met the civil rights leader **Martin Luther King**. In **1967** King nominated him for the **Nobel Peace Prize** and called him an “apostle of peace and non-violence”. The prize was not awarded that year. The two men were united by the conviction that injustice should be fought without violence.

In **1982** he founded the monastery of **Plum Village** in **south-western France**, east of Bordeaux. It became the centre of his worldwide community. His book **“The Miracle of Mindfulness”** of 1975 shows how you can do every activity consciously, even **washing up**. **Mindfulness** means being fully in the moment and noticing what you are doing right now.

In **2005** he received permission to travel to **Vietnam** again. Later he returned to his homeland for good. He spent the last years of his life in the **Tu Hieu** temple in **Hue**, where he had once become a monk. There he died on **22 January 2022** at the age of 95.

gewusst: Thich Nhat Hanh wrote over a hundred books, many of which were translated into numerous languages.
His pupils lovingly called him “Thay”, which in Vietnamese means “teacher”.

teile.einleitung: After the Torah, the Talmud is the most important written work of Judaism. It collects teachings and discussions of rabbis from several centuries. To this day Jews all over the world study its texts.
wichtigste: The Talmud consists of the Mishnah and the Gemara.
The Mishnah was written down around AD 200 under Rabbi Judah the Prince.
The Gemara is mostly written in Aramaic.
There is a Jerusalem Talmud and a Babylonian Talmud; the Babylonian is regarded as authoritative.
The Talmud records the oral Torah in writing.
From the Torah and the Talmud the halakhah is derived, Jewish religious law.
In a yeshiva, the Talmud above all is studied.

abschnitte.text: According to Jewish belief, **Moses** received on Mount Sinai not only the written Torah but also an **oral Torah**. These explanations were for a long time passed on only by word of mouth from teacher to pupil. After the destruction of the Temple in the year 70, the scholars feared that knowledge would be lost. So they began to write the teachings down.

The oldest part is the **Mishnah**. Rabbi **Judah the Prince** had it compiled around AD 200. It is written in **Hebrew** and divided into six great orders. Later, scholars discussed every sentence of the Mishnah at length. These discussions are called the **Gemara** and are written mostly in **Aramaic**, the everyday language of the scholars at that time.

Scholars in the Land of Israel and in **Babylonia**, today’s Iraq, each created a Talmud of their own. The **Jerusalem Talmud** is older and shorter. The **Babylonian Talmud** is much more extensive and was completed later. In Judaism it is regarded as the authoritative one. Anyone who says simply “the Talmud” today usually means it.

The Talmud deals with questions of everyday life and faith: prayer, holidays, food, work, trade and law. From the Torah and the Talmud the **halakhah** is derived, Jewish religious law. The word means roughly “way” or “walking”. In addition, the Talmud contains many stories, parables and pieces of wisdom. Often different opinions are recorded side by side, including those that did not prevail.

In a **yeshiva**, pupils study the Talmud. Often they learn in pairs, discuss out loud and put questions to each other. This way of learning is called **chavruta**. Very important is the commentary of **Rashi**, who lived in the 11th century in Troyes in France. His commentary stands to this day in almost every edition of the Talmud right next to the text.

gewusst: A printed edition of the Babylonian Talmud usually fills around 20 thick volumes.
Many people read one page of the Talmud every day, so a complete cycle takes about seven and a half years.

teile.einleitung: A Zen garden is a Japanese rock garden, usually without water and with only a few plants. Gravel, sand and stones represent a landscape. Such gardens invite quiet contemplation and meditation.
wichtigste: In Japanese a Zen garden is called karesansui, in English a dry landscape garden.
The raked gravel usually represents water and waves.
Stones look like islands or mountains.
In temples, monks rake the patterns anew regularly.
The most famous Zen rock garden lies in the Ryoan-ji temple in Kyoto.
There 15 stones lie, but you never see all of them at once.
Zen Buddhism came from China to Japan in the 12th and 13th centuries.

abschnitte.text: In Japanese a Zen garden is called **karesansui**. That literally means “dry mountain and water landscape”. In English you say **dry landscape garden**. Water is represented there not with real water but with **gravel** or sand. With few means, a whole landscape arises.

The lines in the raked gravel look like **waves** on a lake or sea. The **stones** in it look like islands or mountains. In Zen temples, **monks** rake the patterns anew regularly. For this they use special rakes. This calm, precise work is itself regarded as a form of **meditation**.

The most famous Zen rock garden lies in the **Ryoan-ji** temple in **Kyoto**. It consists of white gravel and **15 stones** in five groups. From any spot on the veranda, however, you see at most **14** of them. What the garden means is not fixed. It belongs to the **UNESCO World Heritage** Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

You usually do not enter a Zen garden. You contemplate it quietly from a **veranda**. It is meant to help you become **calm** and collect yourself. **Zen Buddhism** itself came from **China**, where it is called Chan. Japanese monks brought it to Japan in the 12th and 13th centuries.

In many Japanese temple gardens **moss** grows like a soft green carpet. In the damp gardens of Kyoto in particular, many kinds of moss thrive. Famous is the **moss temple Saiho-ji**. In Japan moss stands for **age** and **calm**. It needs a great deal of care and patience.

gewusst: In Saiho-ji in Kyoto, over a hundred different kinds of moss grow.
Small Zen gardens with sand, stones and a mini rake are today also available for the desk.

teile.einleitung: The Upanishads are ancient philosophical texts from India. They are among the holy scriptures of Hinduism and ask about the self, death and the ground of the world. To this day they influence thinkers in India and Europe.
wichtigste: “Upanishad” means roughly “to sit down close”, like pupils with a teacher.
The Upanishads form the end of the Vedas and are therefore also called Vedanta.
Central are the concepts atman, the self, and Brahman, the ground of the world.
The sentence “Tat tvam asi”, “You are that”, comes from the Chandogya Upanishad.
In the Katha Upanishad, Nachiketa questions Yama, the god of death.
India’s motto “Satyameva Jayate” comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.
Arthur Schopenhauer read them in a Latin translation made from the Persian.

abschnitte.text: The Sanskrit word **Upanishad** is made up of **upa** (near), **ni** (down) and **shad** (sit). So it means roughly “to sit down close”. What is meant is pupils who sit near the teacher for instruction. As the youngest layer, the Upanishads stand at the end of Vedic literature. That is why they are also called **Vedanta**, “end of the Veda”. The oldest are the **Brihadaranyaka Upanishad** and the **Chandogya Upanishad**.

The Upanishads ask what a human being is at the innermost level. The true **self** is called **atman**. The ground of the whole world is called **Brahman**. A central teaching is that atman and Brahman are ultimately one. In the **Chandogya Upanishad** the sage **Uddalaka** instructs his son **Shvetaketu** with the famous sentence **“Tat tvam asi”**, “You are that”. The **Brihadaranyaka Upanishad** describes the Absolute only through negation: **“Neti neti”**, “not this, not this”.

In the **Katha Upanishad** the boy **Nachiketa** comes to **Yama**, the god of death. He is granted three wishes. As his third wish he asks for knowledge of what remains after death. Yama first tries to distract him with riches, but Nachiketa stays firm. Finally Yama teaches him that the true self does not die.

The short **Mandukya Upanishad** has only twelve verses. It interprets the holy syllable **Om** and assigns its sounds to the states of **waking**, **dreaming** and **deep sleep**. The fourth state beyond these it calls **turiya**. From the **Mundaka Upanishad** comes the sentence **“Satyameva Jayate”**, “Truth alone triumphs”. It is the motto of India and stands beneath the state emblem.

In the 17th century the Indian Mughal prince **Dara Shikoh** had the Upanishads translated into **Persian**. Around **1801** the Frenchman **Anquetil-Duperron** rendered this version into **Latin**, under the title “Oupnek’hat”. In this way the German philosopher **Arthur Schopenhauer** came to know the Upanishads. He called them the solace of his life.

gewusst: Traditionally 108 Upanishads are counted, but there are still more texts with this name.
The Upanishads are written in Sanskrit, the ancient holy language of India.

teile.einleitung: Wu wei is an important concept of Daoism, an ancient teaching from China. It is usually translated as “non-action”. But what is meant is not laziness but action without compulsion that follows the natural course of things.
wichtigste: Wu wei literally means “without doing”.
The concept is central in the Daodejing, which is attributed to Laozi.
A famous formula runs: through non-doing, nothing is left undone.
The Daodejing often uses the image of water.
A wise ruler interferes as little as possible in the life of the people.
Closely linked is ziran, natural self-so-ness.

abschnitte.text: **Wu wei** literally means “without doing” and is usually translated as **non-action**. It does not mean that you do nothing at all. It is about acting that is not forced and not tense. You follow the natural course of things instead of fighting against it. Closely linked is the concept of **ziran**, the “self-so-ness” of things.

Wu wei is a central concept in the **Daodejing**. This short book is attributed to the sage **Laozi** and has **81** short chapters. A famous, seemingly contradictory formula runs: **through non-doing, nothing is left undone.** It appears in chapter 48, for example. According to this teaching, it is precisely gentle, unforced action that makes everything succeed.

To explain wu wei, the Daodejing often uses the image of **water**. Water is soft and yielding. Even so, over time it hollows out even hard **stone**. It flows to the lowest places and quarrels with nobody. In this way it shows how much strength lies in gentle working.

Wu wei also applies to **governing**. The ideal ruler interferes **as little** as possible in the life of the people. He governs so unobtrusively that people say everything happened of itself. According to Laozi, too many laws only create unrest. Even **Confucius** praised in the “Analects” the mythical ruler **Shun**, who is said to have governed through non-action.

gewusst: The Daodejing is among the most frequently translated books in the world.
In martial arts such as tai chi too, the idea plays a role of going with the opponent’s movement instead of against it.

teile.einleitung: Syncretism is the name for the mixing of elements of different religions or worldviews. When cultures meet, people often take over gods, customs or teachings from one another. In this way many new forms of belief have arisen over the course of history.
wichtigste: Syncretism means the mixing of different religions.
Plutarch explained the word with the union of the Cretans against an enemy.
The Romans equated foreign gods with their own.
Umbanda in Brazil and Caodaism in Vietnam are examples of mixed religions.
In Haitian Vodou, spirit beings are often equated with Catholic saints.
The term can be used neutrally as a description or disparagingly.

abschnitte.text: The Greek writer **Plutarch** described how quarrelling Cretans allied themselves against outside enemies. He called this union **synkretismos**. Later the term was transferred to the **mixing of religions**. In the 17th century the Lutheran theologian **Georg Calixt** stood at the centre of the so-called syncretistic controversy. He sought an understanding between the denominations, while his opponents accused him of mixing the teachings improperly.

In their great empire the Romans met many foreign peoples. They often interpreted those peoples’ gods as forms of their own gods. In Germanic or Celtic gods, for example, they saw **Mercury** or **Mars**. This practice is called **interpretatio Romana**. The expression goes back to the Roman historian **Tacitus**.

**Umbanda** arose at the beginning of the 20th century in Rio de Janeiro. It combines Afro-Brazilian traditions with Catholicism and spiritism. In Haitian **Vodou** the spirit beings are called **lwa**, and they are often shown in the images of Catholic saints. In Mexico, in 1531, the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have appeared on the hill of **Tepeyac**. There had previously been a sanctuary of the Aztec goddess Tonantzin, which is why the place is often cited as an example of religious overlaying.

**Caodaism** was founded in Vietnam in 1926. It unites elements from Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism and Christianity. Unusually, it also reveres famous people as saints. Among them is the French writer **Victor Hugo**. There he is regarded as a spirit being who passes on messages.

Some use the word syncretism **disparagingly**, as if a religion were thereby less genuine. Scholars of religion stress, by contrast, that almost all religions have taken in elements from other traditions. They therefore usually use the term **neutrally**, to describe such processes. Christianity in Europe, too, took older customs into its festivals, for example.

gewusst: In Caodaism in Vietnam, the French poet Victor Hugo is revered as a saint.
The word syncretism originally meant an alliance of Cretans, not a religion.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Egypt people believed that every person comes before a court after death. At the judgement of the dead, the heart of the deceased was weighed. Only someone who had lived well was allowed to move on to the afterlife.
wichtigste: At the judgement of the dead, the heart of the deceased was placed on a scale.
In the other pan lay the feather of the goddess Maat.
Anubis with the jackal head operated the scale.
Thoth, the god of scribes, wrote down the result.
The monster Ammit devoured the heart of a bad person.
The deceased had to declare his innocence before 42 judges.

abschnitte.text: The ancient Egyptians believed that the **heart** is the seat of **reason** and **conscience**. That is why at the **judgement of the dead** the heart of the deceased was placed on a **scale**. In the other pan lay the **feather of Maat**. **Maat** was the goddess of **truth** and **order**. A good heart must not be heavier than her feather.

The god **Anubis** with the **jackal head** operated the scale. He was the god of **embalming** and accompanied the dead into the afterlife. Beside the scale stood **Thoth**, the god of scribes and wisdom. He was often shown with an **ibis head**. Thoth wrote down the result of the weighing. **Osiris**, the ruler of the afterlife, presided.

According to **Spell 125** of the **Book of the Dead**, a court of **42 gods** sat in judgement. Before each of these judges the deceased had to deny a particular sin. He said, for example: “I have not stolen” or “I have not lied”. The **Book of the Dead** is a collection of spells that were put into the grave with the dead. They were meant to help them pass the judgement.

Beside the scale waited the monster **Ammit**. She was a composite creature made of **crocodile**, **lion** and **hippopotamus**. If the heart was too heavy, Ammit devoured it. Then the deceased was lost for ever. Anyone who passed the judgement was allowed to move on to the **Field of Reeds**, a beautiful land in the afterlife, like Egypt with fertile fields.

gewusst: Many pictures of the judgement of the dead are on papyrus scrolls that were found in tombs and now lie in museums.
The Egyptians often laid a stone scarab on the heart of the mummy so that it would not speak against the deceased at the judgement.

teile.einleitung: Zoroastrianism is a very old religion from the area of present-day Iran. It goes back to the prophet Zarathustra. At its centre is the struggle between truth and falsehood, and every person is to choose the good freely.
wichtigste: Zoroastrianism goes back to the prophet Zarathustra.
Asha stands for truth and order, Druj for falsehood and chaos.
The principle is: good thoughts, good words, good deeds.
After death every soul crosses the Chinvat Bridge.
At the end of time the saviour Saoshyant is to appear.
The holy texts are called the Avesta.

abschnitte.text: Zoroastrianism is named after the prophet **Zarathustra**, in Greek **Zoroaster**. When exactly he lived is disputed among experts. The faithful revere the creator god **Ahura Mazda**. Their holy texts are called the **Avesta**. **Fire** is regarded as a sign of purity and burns in the fire temples.

Zoroastrianism describes the world as a struggle between two forces. **Asha** stands for truth and cosmic order. **Druj** stands for falsehood and chaos. Experts speak of an **ethical dualism**. Every person is to decide for Asha by **free choice** and so stand on the side of good.

The most important principle of Zoroastrian ethics has three parts: **good thoughts, good words, good deeds**. In Avestan it is called **Humata, Hukhta, Hvarshta**. It sums up how a person should live rightly. So it is not enough only to think good things: speaking and acting count too.

After death every soul must cross the **Chinvat Bridge**. For the righteous it becomes wide and leads to paradise. For liars it becomes narrow as a blade. At the end of time the saviour **Saoshyant** is to appear. He is to raise the dead, finally defeat evil and renew the world.

gewusst: Today only a few Zoroastrians remain, and many of them live as Parsis in India.
Ideas such as a judgment after death and a saviour at the end of time also exist in other religions.

teile.einleitung: The First Zionist Congress took place at the end of August 1897 in Basel. There Jewish delegates from many countries founded the Zionist Organization. Its aim was a secure homeland for the Jewish people in Palestine.
wichtigste: The First Zionist Congress met from 29 to 31 August 1897 in Basel.
The meeting place was the music hall of the Stadtcasino Basel.
The congress was actually supposed to take place in Munich.
Theodor Herzl was elected president of the new organization.
The Basel Programme demanded a homeland in Palestine secured under public law.
Between 1897 and 1946 the congress met ten times in Basel.

abschnitte.text: **Zionism** is a political movement that arose at the end of the 19th century. Its name comes from **Zion**, a hill in Jerusalem that stands for the Land of Israel. Many Jews in Europe were then suffering from exclusion and hostility. The journalist **Theodor Herzl** from Vienna therefore wanted to create a safe homeland for the Jewish people.

Herzl first planned the congress in **Munich**. The Jewish community there and the association of rabbis in Germany, however, resisted this. So the organizers moved to **Basel**. From 29 to 31 August 1897, around 200 delegates met in the **music hall of the Stadtcasino**. A commemorative plaque recalls this today.

The congress adopted the **Basel Programme**. It demanded a **homeland secured under public law** for the Jewish people in Palestine. The word “homeland” was deliberately chosen to be more cautious than “state”. The programme became the founding text of the Zionist Organization, later called the World Zionist Organization. Herzl became its first president.

Basel remained closely linked with Zionism. Between 1897 and 1946 the city hosted the congress **ten times**, more often than any other city. Since 1951, that is, after the founding of the State of Israel, the congress has met in **Jerusalem**. In 2022 a celebration of the **125th anniversary** of the First Congress took place in Basel.

gewusst: After the congress, Herzl wrote in his diary that in Basel he had founded the Jewish state.
Basel hosted the Zionist Congress more often than any other city.

teile.einleitung: A taboo is something that you must not do, must not touch or must not say. The word comes from Polynesia and had a religious meaning there. Today we also use it in everyday life.
wichtigste: The word taboo comes from Tonga in Polynesia, where it is “tapu”.
Originally it means something sacred that is at the same time forbidden.
James Cook noted the word in 1777 in Tonga and made it known in Europe.
According to old belief, anyone who breaks a taboo comes to harm, even without punishment by people.
Sigmund Freud wrote the book “Totem and Taboo” in 1913.
Today topics that people prefer not to talk about are also called a taboo.

abschnitte.titel: A word from the South Seas
abschnitte.text: The word **tapu** comes from the language of **Tonga**, a group of islands in the Pacific. Similar words exist in many Polynesian languages, for example in Hawaii or among the Maori in New Zealand. It denotes something that is set apart and may not simply be touched. This could be a place, an object, a food or even a person, for example a chief.

In the original sense a taboo is **at once holy and dangerous**. People imagined that the taboo is charged with a supernatural power. According to this idea, anyone who breaks it brings misfortune on themselves, even if nobody punishes them. The taboo thus protects the sacred from the everyday and people from a power they cannot control.

abschnitte.titel: How the word came to Europe
abschnitte.text: The English seafarer **James Cook** visited the islands of Tonga in 1777 on his third great voyage. He wrote the word as “taboo” in his travel journal. His account of the voyage was widely read, and so the word passed into English, German and many other languages. Researchers soon used it for similar prohibitions in cultures all over the world.

Many researchers asked where taboos come from. The doctor **Sigmund Freud** published the book “Totem and Taboo” in 1913. In it he combined reports by ethnologists with his **psychoanalysis**, that is, his teaching about the unconscious. His explanations are regarded in **ethnology** (the study of peoples) today as speculative and outdated. But the book made the word better known still.

Today in everyday life we also say: “That is taboo.” What is meant is something you must not do or would rather not talk about. Such taboos differ from country to country and from time to time. What used to be taboo can often be discussed openly today. Sometimes it helps to break a taboo so that people can talk about a difficult subject.

gewusst: In Tonga it used to be forbidden to touch the head or the belongings of a high chief.
The opposite of tapu is called “noa” in many Polynesian languages; it means roughly “ordinary” or “free”.

teile.einleitung: A torii is a large gate that stands at the entrance to a Shinto shrine. It is one of the best-known landmarks of Japan. Anyone who goes through a torii enters a holy area.
wichtigste: A torii is a gate at the entrance to a Shinto shrine.
Almost all torii are in Japan.
Many torii are painted bright orange-red.
Most torii are made of wood, some of stone or metal.
A torii usually has two vertical posts and two crossbeams.
The great torii of Miyajima stands in the sea.
At the Fushimi Inari shrine in Kyoto, thousands of torii stand one behind another.

abschnitte.text: A **torii** stands at the entrance to a **Shinto shrine**. **Shinto** is the old native religion of Japan, in which many deities are revered, the **kami**. The torii marks the boundary between the everyday world and the holy area of the shrine. Many people bow briefly before they go through. Because torii belong to Shinto shrines, almost all of them stand in **Japan**.

A torii usually has **two vertical posts**. On top lie **two crossbeams**, and the upper one is often curved slightly upwards. Most torii are made of **wood**, but there are also torii of **stone**, concrete or metal. Many are painted bright **orange-red**. This colour is meant to keep misfortune away, and the paint also protects the wood from rotting.

On the island of **Miyajima**, the great torii of the **Itsukushima Shrine** stands in the sea. At **high tide** it seems to float on the water. At **low tide** you can walk to the gate on foot. The shrine is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and one of the most famous places in Japan.

At the **Fushimi Inari shrine** in **Kyoto**, **thousands of torii** stand close one behind another. They form long orange-red **tunnels** leading up the mountain. Many of these torii were donated by companies and families. Their name is written on the posts. The shrine is dedicated to the deity **Inari**, whose messengers are **foxes**. That is why you see many stone fox figures there.

gewusst: On Japanese maps a Shinto shrine is marked with the symbol of a small torii.
The torii of Miyajima is not fixed in the seabed; it stays up through its own great weight.

teile.einleitung: The Yasukuni Shrine is a shrine of the Shinto religion in Tokyo. It commemorates the people who died in wars in the service of Japan. It is one of the most controversial places in East Asia.
wichtigste: The shrine stands in the Chiyoda district of Tokyo, near the Imperial Palace.
It was founded in 1869 under the name Tokyo Shokonsha.
Since 1879 it has been called Yasukuni, roughly “peaceful country”.
It commemorates around 2.5 million war dead.
In 1978, 14 convicted major war criminals were enshrined.
Visits by Japanese prime ministers set off protests in China and South Korea.
On the grounds stands the war museum Yushukan.

abschnitte.text: The shrine was founded in **1869** under Emperor **Meiji**. It was first called **Tokyo Shokonsha** and was intended for those who fell in the **Boshin War**. In **1879** it received the name **Yasukuni**. It goes back to a classical Chinese expression and means roughly **“peaceful country”**. The shrine lies in the **Chiyoda** district in the centre of **Tokyo**.

In Shinto it is believed that the souls of the dead can be revered as **kami**. In the Yasukuni Shrine the souls of the war dead are revered. The register names over **2.46 million** people. Most of them died in the **Pacific War** of 1941 to 1945. For many families in Japan the shrine is a place of mourning.

In **1978**, in a secret ceremony, **14** men were enshrined who had been charged after the war as Class A **major war criminals**. Among them was the former prime minister **Hideki Tojo**. Since then, visits by politicians have been very controversial. **China** and **South Korea** in particular protest, because they suffered greatly under the Japanese occupation. Supporters say it is only about remembering the dead, while critics see it as playing down the past.

On the grounds stands the war museum **Yushukan**. It shows weapons, letters and keepsakes from Japan’s wars. Critics accuse the museum of presenting history in a **whitewashed** way. The museum itself sees its task as showing the view of the fallen. This too is disputed in Japan and abroad.

In the shrine stands a special **cherry tree** of the **Somei-Yoshino** variety. It serves the Japanese **weather agency** as a reference tree. When enough blossoms on it are open, the start of the **cherry blossom season** in Tokyo is officially announced. Every spring this is news across the whole country.

gewusst: Since 1975 no Japanese emperor has visited the Yasukuni Shrine.
Since 1946 the shrine has no longer belonged to the state but is a private religious institution.

teile.einleitung: Yin and yang is an ancient idea from China. It describes two opposites that belong together and complement each other. The well-known black and white sign is seen all over the world today.
wichtigste: Yin and yang comes from China.
The idea is especially important in Daoism.
The sign is a circle with a black and a white half.
In each half there is a dot of the other colour.
Yang stands for light and warmth, yin for darkness and coolness.
Yin and yang show that opposites belong together.

abschnitte.text: The yin and yang sign is a **circle**. A curved line divides it into a **black** and a **white** half. The halves look like two drops embracing each other. In the black half lies a **white dot**, in the white half a **black** one. This shows: in each there is a little of the other.

The idea of yin and yang is very old and comes from **China**. It is especially important in **Daoism**, but also plays a role in other Chinese teachings. Traditional **Chinese medicine** also uses the two terms. There a person is supposed to be healthy when yin and yang are in **balance**.

**Yang** is the bright, warm, active side. It is often linked with the **sun** and the day. **Yin** is the dark, cool, calm side. It is linked with the **moon** and the night. Neither side is better than the other. They need each other.

Yin and yang show that **opposites** belong together and **complement** each other. A good example is **day and night**: they take turns, and one passes into the other. Summer and winter or rest and movement fit too. According to this idea, everything in the world is constantly in **change**.

gewusst: The yin and yang sign can be seen on the flag of South Korea, there in red and blue.
The word yin originally meant the shady side of a mountain, and yang the sunny side.

teile.einleitung: The Zohar is the most important book of Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism. It explains the Torah in a mysterious way and speaks about God, the world and the soul. Its name means “splendour”.
wichtigste: The Zohar is the main work of Kabbalah.
The Hebrew title means “splendour”.
Traditionally it is attributed to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai of the 2nd century.
According to present-day research, Moses de León wrote it in the late 13th century in Castile.
The scholar Gershom Scholem contributed much to this insight.

abschnitte.text: The Hebrew word **Zohar** means **splendour**. The title alludes to a verse in the **Book of Daniel**: there it says that the wise will shine like the splendour of the heavens. The Zohar is the main work of **Kabbalah**, Jewish mysticism. It interprets the texts of the **Torah** and seeks in them a hidden, deeper meaning.

In the Zohar, Rabbi **Shimon bar Yochai**, a scholar of the 2nd century, appears as a teacher with his students. That is why tradition regards him as the author, and many devout people still see it this way today. Research came to a different result: from about 1280, **Moses de León** circulated the Zohar in **Castile** in Spain. The scholar **Gershom Scholem** showed that Moses de León was probably also the main author.

The Zohar is written largely in **Aramaic**. It became one of the most influential books of Judaism. Many later Kabbalists built on it. To this day, people who are interested in Jewish mysticism read and study it.

gewusst: The Zohar is written in an ancient language that was spoken in the time of Shimon bar Yochai, although it arose much later.

teile.einleitung: The Dreamtime is a central part of the belief of the Aboriginal people, the indigenous inhabitants of Australia. Its stories tell how ancestral beings shaped the world. These stories have been passed on for a very long time.
wichtigste: The Dreamtime belongs to the belief of the Aboriginal people in Australia.
The Aboriginal people have lived in Australia for many tens of thousands of years.
In the Dreamtime, ancestral beings shaped the land, the animals and the plants.
The Rainbow Serpent is said to have shaped rivers and waterholes.
The stories are passed on by telling, singing, dancing and painting.
Dreaming tracks or songlines are sung paths through the land.
For the Aboriginal people the land is sacred.

abschnitte.text: The **Aboriginal people** are the **indigenous inhabitants of Australia**. They have lived there for many **tens of thousands of years** and have one of the oldest living cultures in the world. There are many different groups with languages and stories of their own. Common to many of them is the belief in the **Dreamtime**, in English “Dreamtime” or “the Dreaming”.

In the **Dreamtime**, **ancestral beings** moved across the still empty earth. They shaped the **land**, the **animals** and the **plants**. A particularly mighty ancestral being is the **Rainbow Serpent**. It is said to have shaped rivers and waterholes. The ancestral beings also gave people **rules** for living. For the Aboriginal people the Dreamtime is not only the past; it still has an effect today.

The paths along which the ancestral beings wandered are called **dreaming tracks** or **songlines**. Each section has a song. With these songs people could remember their way through the vast land, for example to waterholes. Because every mountain, river and rock has a story from the Dreamtime, the **land is sacred** to the Aboriginal people.

The stories of the Dreamtime have been passed on **orally** for a very long time. **Songs**, **dances** and **pictures** help in remembering. Typical of many Aboriginal people is **dot painting**: pictures made of many small dots of colour that show stories and landscapes. The **didgeridoo** also comes from the Aboriginal people. It is a long wind instrument made from a branch hollowed out by termites, and it sounds deep and droning.

gewusst: Some Aboriginal rock paintings are many thousands of years old.
Uluru in the middle of Australia is, for the Anangu who live there, a holy place with many stories from the Dreamtime.

teile.einleitung: Theravada is the oldest surviving school of Buddhism. The name means “teaching of the elders”. It is widespread above all in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.
wichtigste: Theravada means “teaching of the elders”.
The holy scriptures are written in Pali, an ancient Indian language.
The collection of scriptures is called the Tipitaka, “three baskets”.
In Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, Theravada is the most important religion.
The ideal is the arahant, who has reached nirvana.
Monks and monastery life carry especially great weight.
The community of monks and nuns is called the sangha.

abschnitte.text: The name **Theravada** means **“teaching of the elders”**. The school sees itself as the keeper of the original teaching of the **Buddha**. In the past, followers of **Mahayana** described the older schools with the word **Hinayana**, “small vehicle”. This term is regarded as disparaging. Today people mostly speak of Theravada or of the early schools.

The holy scriptures of Theravada are written in **Pali**, an ancient Indian language. The collection is called the **Tipitaka**, literally **“three baskets”**. It consists of three “baskets”: the **monastic rules** for monks and nuns, the **discourses** of the Buddha and the **philosophical texts**. It is also called the **Pali Canon**. The texts were first passed on orally and later written down in Sri Lanka.

Theravada is the predominant religion above all in **Sri Lanka**. In **Thailand**, **Myanmar**, **Cambodia** and **Laos** too it is the most important form of Buddhism. There are many monasteries and temples there. In Europe, including Switzerland, there are also a few Theravada monasteries today.

In Theravada the aim is to become an **arahant** yourself, a “worthy one”. An arahant has reached **nirvana** and is freed from the cycle of **rebirths**. The path there leads through ethics, meditation and wisdom. Every person has to walk this path by their own effort.

**Monastery life** carries great weight in Theravada, because it is regarded as the best path to liberation. The monks are regarded as role models. The community of monks and nuns is called the **sangha**. Together with the **Buddha** and the teaching, the **dharma**, it is one of the **“Three Jewels”** in which Buddhists take refuge. **Lay people** support the monks with food and gifts.

gewusst: Theravada monks traditionally eat only in the morning and after that nothing solid until the next morning.
